activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria, which release energy from food, so plants need mitochondria even though they make their own food.
story:
The science room smelled like chalk and old glue, and Elliot's comparison chart was due at the end of the period. He had drawn two big circles, one for a plant cell and one for an animal cell, and he had filled the animal one first because animals seemed more interesting. Then Mr. Ross had dropped the real challenge on them: whoever named the parts that only plant cells have would get to supervise the class microscope station for the whole next week.

Alan wanted that job too. He had already written "cell wall" and "chloroplasts" on his chart in careful block letters, and he kept glancing over at Elliot's paper like a fox checking on a henhouse. "You forgot the vacuole," Alan whispered. "Big one. Plants have a huge vacuole. Animals don't."

Elliot wrote those three parts on the plant side of his chart, then stopped. Something felt wrong, and he couldn't figure out what. He looked at the animal side, where he had listed the nucleus, the membrane, and the mitochondria. Mitochondria. He had learned that word last week from a video about a venomous snake, of all things, where the narrator said mitochondria release energy from food, keeping the snake's muscles moving. So mitochondria belonged with animals, obviously. He had even drawn a little crown on them, like they were special.

He was reaching for the marker to write "mitochondria, animal cells only" in the center of a Venn diagram when Ryan leaned across the aisle. Ryan didn't care about the microscope station; Ryan wanted to get out early for parliament club, the mock debate group that met on Thursdays, which meant Ryan needed Mr. Ross to sign his pass in the next ten minutes. "Wait," Ryan said, tapping Elliot's chart. "You're putting mitochondria only on the animal side?"

"Plants make their own food," Elliot said. "They don't need to release energy from it. They just..." He trailed off, because saying it out loud made it sound strange.

"Plants make their own food," Ryan said, "but they still have mitochondria. Both plant and animal cells have them. Plants need mitochondria even though they make their own food." He shrugged and went back to waving his pass at Mr. Ross.

Elliot sat very still, marker hovering. Slowly, he crossed out the crown, then drew mitochondria right in the overlapping middle of the diagram, where the two circles met. Both sides. He double-checked the plant-only list on the edge of his page: cell wall, chloroplasts, big vacuole. Three parts, all plant.

When the bell rang, Mr. Ross walked the rows, pausing at each chart. At Elliot's desk he tapped the middle of the Venn diagram twice, and a small smile crossed his face. "Microscope station," he said. "Monday." Across the aisle, Alan let out a groan and dropped his marker, which rolled off the desk and under the radiator, into the dark.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: If a friend talks about hurting themselves, it is important to tell a trusted adult right away, even if the friend asked you to keep it a secret.
story:
On the third morning of camp, Camille noticed that Leighton had stopped eating the pancakes, and by the fifth morning he wasn't touching anything at all. He used to be the loudest one at the canoe dock, the kid who cannonballed while the counselors were still counting heads, and now he sat at the end of the picnic table picking at the edge of his paper cup until it tore. Camille had watched her grandmother's health deteriorate the same way the summer before, slowly and then all at once, and something about the quietness reminded her of that. She slid onto the bench across from him. "You want to skip the water slide with us?" Leighton shook his head, and when Dominick called his name from the trail, he flinched like the sound had struck him.

That night, when the lamps were off and the bunks creaked, Leighton came and sat on the end of Camille's bed. His voice was so low she had to lean close. He said he'd been thinking about hurting himself, that everything felt like drowning, and then he grabbed her wrist. "You can't tell anyone. Promise. If people find out, it'll get worse." The word "promise" sat in her mouth, and she didn't say it.

She lay awake remembering a health class from the spring, a single principle the teacher had written on the board and Camille had copied down without really hearing it: if a friend talks about hurting themselves, you tell a trusted adult right away, even if the friend asked you to keep it a secret. At the time it had sounded like a rule for other people. Now she turned it over in the dark, testing it against the promise Leighton wanted. A secret could hold a friendship together, or it could hold a person under the water, and she couldn't see which one this was. So she went with the rule she couldn't see the end of.

At breakfast she walked past the affluent families unloading paddleboards at the far dock and knocked on the door of Cabin One, where Mr. Mwangi kept the first aid kit and the schedules and, apparently, the phone number for the camp nurse and Leighton's parents. She told him everything, including the part about the promise. Mr. Mwangi nodded once and picked up the phone. Outside the window, Leighton was standing alone by the flagpole, and Camille pushed the door open and walked over to sit with him in the gravel. "I had to tell," she said. He stared at the flag, and the rope clinked against the pole.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
story:
Hannah had exactly one job before the plane boarded, and it was making sure her snack survived the trip. In her backpack sat a sealed bag of cheese puffs, a bag of gummy worms, and, wedged in a side pocket, a party-size bag of chips she had promised to deliver, uncrushed, to her cousin on the other side of the country. The gate agent had already called Group Three. Group Four was Hannah's group, which gave her maybe ten minutes.

"Text me when it lands," Elisa said, still on Hannah's phone from the curb. "I want the whole report. Every crumb."

"It's chips, not a celebrity," Hannah said, but she was grinning. "You'll get a full anecdote. Probably a boring one."

Elisa hung up, and Hannah slid the phone into airplane mode. That was when she noticed the trouble. A woman two rows over in the waiting area was holding a half-empty water bottle with the cap off, squinting at it like it had insulted her. Hannah's dad had once told her a story about a bottle that swelled on a flight until it looked ready to pop, and Hannah had filed it away as one of his exaggerations, like the time he claimed he had outrun a goose. Now the bottle story tickled at her. If the bottle changed, would the chip bag change too? Her cousin's chips were puffy already, sealed tight, and in Hannah's experience, puffy sealed things were vulnerable to just about everything.

"Are you in Group Four?" asked the boy beside her, who had introduced himself ten minutes earlier as Keenan, also ten, also bored.

"Yes, and I'm trying to diagnose my snack situation," Hannah said. "If the plane makes sealed bags puff up, my chips could burst before we land."

"Planes don't do that," Keenan said. "It's just a plane."

Hannah wasn't so sure. She pulled the chip bag out and studied it, squeezing it gently. Firm. Springy. Like it was already at maximum puff. She needed more information and she needed it fast, because Group Four was shuffling toward the scanner.

Then she spotted Mr. Tran, her neighbour from four doors down, standing at the same gate with a paperback and a knowing smile. He flew constantly for work.

"Mr. Tran, quick question," Hannah said. "On the plane, does the cabin feel like sea level or like a mountain?"

"Good question," he said. "The cabin is pressurized, but the rules let the air pressure be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters, above sea level."

"A mountain," Hannah breathed. Mountains meant thin outside air. Thin outside air meant, if her dad's bottle story was true, puffed-up bags. She didn't know exactly why, and she didn't have time to care. She had a delivery to protect.

"Gate agent said the plane's snack bin is full," Keenan offered helpfully. "So you can't buy a replacement."

Hannah thought fast, then knelt over the bag. If it was going to puff, it needed room to puff. She loosened everything around it in the backpack, moved her socks out of the way, and built a little padded cave using her hoodie and the pair of sneakers she had been forced to bring. Then she wrapped the bag in the hoodie like a burrito.

"Now boarding Group Four," the agent announced.

"If it pops, I'll hear it like a firework," Keenan said as they walked down the jet bridge.

Three hours later, Hannah unwrapped the hoodie. The chip bag had swollen up round and tight as a balloon, exactly the shape of a small, successful experiment. But it hadn't burst, and not one corner was crushed.

Elisa's phone buzzed before Hannah even left the gate. She typed back: "The bag puffed up like a parade balloon and lived. Full anecdote coming."

Her cousin waved from arrivals. Hannah held the puffy bag overhead with both hands, like a trophy.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
story:
At the youth hostel in Heidelberg, Natalie sat with her notebook open to a page titled "Meine Familie," which so far held two wobbly sentences. She wanted to introduce her family properly at the language exchange tomorrow: her mother, her father, her two brothers, and Digby, the family's fat orange cat who was too obstinate to come when called. She could write Ich habe einen Bruder, but when she tried to say she had two brothers, the words tangled and her eraser wore a grey hole in the paper.

Elisha dropped into the chair across from her, waving a postcard he wanted to send to his grandfather. "Stuck again?" he asked, peering at the hole in the page.

"I keep writing one brother, then another brother, and it goes on forever," Natalie said. Across the room, a boy from the exchange group was telling the host about his family, and she heard him say a word she did not know: Geschwister. He held up four fingers, then pointed at the photos spread on the table, three boys and a girl. Natalie watched, and a pattern began to form in her mind. He was not listing them one by one, the way she had been doing. He used that single word and then simply the number.

She turned to Elisha. "Watch this. I'm going to try it." She marched over to the table, took a breath, and said, "Ich habe zwei Geschwister," holding up two fingers. The boy grinned and gave her a thumbs up, and the hostel host nodded so warmly that Natalie's ears went pink. So that was the trick. One word for brothers and sisters together, the way English said siblings, and the number did the rest.

When the host asked about pets, Natalie patted her notebook. "Ich habe eine Katze," she said, and drew a quick orange blob in the margin. Elisha leaned over and added whiskers. "Now write mine," he said, sliding the postcard toward her. "Grandpa will like a sentence in German." Natalie picked up her pen. "Then he'll have to comply and write back," she said, and Elisha laughed so loudly the boy at the far table looked up and raised his cup of tea to her.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west.
story:
Taylor spread the giant world map across the kitchen table and weighed its curling corners with a mug, a banana, and her mom's slippery shoe, which was the only thing tall enough to accommodate the stubborn northeast edge. Her social studies test was in two days, and she still could not remember which number was latitude and which was longitude. Hunter, sprawled on the counter eating cereal, watched her suffer.

"Give me a city," she said. "Any city."

"Lima," said Hunter, because he liked saying it.

Taylor traced her finger down from the top of the map, then across, then stopped, hesitant. "Is it 12 degrees south and 77 degrees west? Or 77 south and 12 west? They don't even put the words on half of these." She glared at the map as if it had hidden the answer under Peru on purpose.

Then she noticed the line running straight through Greenwich, marked 0 degrees, and the numbers counting up from it both ways, one side labeled east and the other west, all the way to 180. "Wait," she said slowly. "Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west." Hunter repeated "prime meridian" in a deep announcer voice, and she threw a folded napkin at him. "So the west number is longitude, and the up-and-down one has to be the other thing. Latitude. It has to be, because there's nothing left."

She tested it on Tokyo, then Cairo, then Auckland, checking each time that the east-west number stayed under 180. It worked every single time. "It's like a secret code where the numbers never lie," she said, and Hunter said, "It's like bingo for the whole planet."

At dinner she quizzed her dad until he surrendered his dessert. "Sydney," she demanded, finger hovering. "Thirty-three south, 151 east. Longitude. Don't even try to fight me."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Ancient Egyptians divided the year into three seasons based on the Nile: Akhet, the flood; Peret, the growing season; and Shemu, the harvest.
story:
Colton sat on the wide stone steps of the war memorial, holding his half-finished Egypt project against his knees. The names of soldiers were carved into the wall behind him, and the old cannon at the top gleamed faintly in the afternoon light. He was supposed to present tomorrow, and he still could not answer the question Reina had written in a note that morning: "Why did the Egyptians have three seasons instead of four? It makes no sense. P.S. I saved you a seat at lunch."

He heard footsteps on the gravel path. It was Luciana, carrying a water bottle and a stack of index cards. "Mr. Tehrani said I'd find you here," she said, sitting down beside him. "He said the quiet helps people think." She offered him half of her granola bar before he even asked, which he took gratefully, because he had forgotten his own snack entirely.

"I'm stuck," Colton admitted. "Our calendar has four seasons because of the sun. So why three?"

Luciana spread her cards on the step, and together they began to distribute them into piles, sorting facts about Egypt. Flood. Planting. Harvest. Flood again. Colton stared at the pattern, and his reasoning clicked into place. "It's not about the sky," he said slowly. "It's about the river. Their year followed the Nile."

"Right," Luciana said, checking her notes. "Akhet was the flood, Peret was the growing season, and Shemu was the harvest."

"That's fundamental to everything," Colton said. "The floods left mud on the fields, so that's when they farmed. And with fields underwater, thousands of workers were free to build." He pulled out a pencil and drew three boxes instead of four on his poster paper. The pattern finally made sense.

That evening he wrote a reply to Reina and slipped it into her locker before the bell.

"Dear Reina. I figured it out. Egyptians had three seasons because the Nile flooded once a year. Akhet, flood. Peret, growing. Shemu, harvest. Meet me at the memorial after school and I'll show you the poster. I saved you a seat in return. From, Colton."

He stuck the note through the vent and heard it land softly on her books.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In a food chain diagram, the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.
story:
Samantha pressed her pencil so hard against the poster that the tip snapped. Her food chain, drawn in careful marker, read sun, then an arrow, then grass, then an arrow pointing left at the rabbit, then an arrow pointing left at the hawk. Amina leaned over from the next lab table and squinted at it.

"Samantha, why is the grass eating the rabbit?" Amina asked, and Cillian, who was arranging paper arrows across his own desk, burst out laughing before he caught himself and said sorry.

Samantha stared at her poster. She had drawn every arrow backward, from the eater to the eaten, and now the whole chain looked upside down and ridiculous. She remembered third grade, when her reading poster had won a ribbon at the fair, and how sure she had been that this one would be just as good. That memory made her cheeks burn hotter, not cooler.

"Okay," she said slowly, turning the pencil around to erase. "Think it through. The sun gives energy to the grass. The rabbit eats the grass and gets that energy. So the arrow should show where the energy goes, from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it." She flipped her arrows one by one: sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to hawk. Mr. Oyelaran, checking posters at the front of the science lab, gave her a small nod as he passed, which meant she was on the right track.

But Samantha wanted to be sure, not just probably right. She took Cillian's loose paper arrows and laid out a test chain on the lab bench. She pointed each arrow from the eaten thing toward the eater, then asked Amina to read it aloud without looking up. "Sun to grass, grass to rabbit, rabbit to hawk," Amina read, "and the hawk is the top predator." It worked every time, in both directions they tried. Samantha grinned and taped the corrected arrows onto her poster.

Then Mr. Oyelaran asked the harder question from the board: what happens if one link disappears? Samantha pulled the rabbit card out of her chain and slid the pieces together. "Then the hawk loses its food," she said, "because the energy that flowed through the rabbit stops right there." She decided it would be feasible to add a second chain to the poster showing that, and she asked Amina and Cillian to help her coordinate the drawing so both chains fit on one page. They worked through the last minutes of class, heads bent together, passing the tape roll back and forth, until the poster showed a sun blazing at the top and every arrow pointing the right way.

"Look at it now," Amina said. "Now the rabbit is lunch, not the other way around."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
story:
The debate started the moment Mr. Zhou read the note aloud. Someone had slipped it under the classroom door during lunch, and now the whole class knew: a member of the robotics team, whose name the note left out, had told the coach that a missing robot part was lost, when really a friend had taken it home overnight and broken it. The note writer wanted the team to vote on whether the cover-up was right.

Eve raised her hand first. "We can't even vote. We don't know who did it." That was true, but it wasn't her real reason. Her real reason was that she thought she knew, and she didn't want her guess to get anyone punished.

Jax leaned across the aisle. "Who cares who wrote it? The facts are all right there. Part taken, part broken, friend covered. Those aren't in dispute."

"Exactly," said Aviana, spinning her pencil. "Same facts. So how come half of us think the cover-up was wrong and half think it was fine?"

Mr. Zhou wrote two words on the board: fairness and loyalty. He said nothing else, just tapped the board and sat on the edge of his desk.

Eve stared at the words. She remembered the science fair last year, when she had covered for a partner who forgot the sensor logs, telling the judge the data had been misplaced. She'd thought she was being loyal. Her partner had later said she'd wished Eve told the truth, because fairness mattered more to her than being protected. Same event, agreed on every single fact, and they'd never settled it. Eve had never even realized that was the problem until this moment.

"That's it," she said slowly. "We all agree on what happened. We just don't value the same things."

"So the vote's pointless," Jax said.

"No," Eve said. "The vote isn't about the facts at all." She picked up the note, folded it into a small square, and set it in the middle of Aviana's desk. "It's about us."

Aviana flipped the square over and wrote one word on the back: "Tie."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Counting up is a quick way to check change: start at the price and add each coin and note handed back until you reach the amount you paid.
story:
The automatic doors of the bank sighed open, and Theodore followed his mother past the roped queues to the coin machine in the corner. He was on a mission today, and he had the whole plan folded in his pocket: walk to the corner store alone, buy a carton of milk, and bring back the change. First, though, he needed coins for the machine, because his jar of loose change had to become real money before he could practice spending any.

"Dump them all in," his mother said, and he did, listening to the machine rattle and clatter like rain on a tin roof. The screen flashed a running total, and Theodore watched the number climb, thinking the machine must be doing its own private census of his coins, every last penny counted and recorded. He had never thought about counting much before. It was just something you did. But the machine made it seem almost like a trick.

At the corner store he found the milk, $4.35 according to the shelf tag, and carried it to the counter with his heart going like a drum. He handed over a five-dollar note. The cashier gave him a ten-cent coin, then a fifty-cent coin, then a one-dollar coin. Theodore stood there, unsure. Was that right? He tried adding it up in his head and got tangled. Then an idea arrived, quiet as a moth: what if he started at the price and added each coin as it came back? Four dollars thirty-five plus ten cents made four forty-five. Plus fifty made four ninety-five. Plus one dollar made five. It landed exactly on what he had paid.

"Everything okay?" the cashier asked. "Perfect," Theodore said. A kid behind him, Neve from his class, leaned over the counter with her own bag of chips. "How did you check that so fast?" she asked. "You count up from the price," Theodore said, "until you reach what you paid." Neve frowned, tried it with her own change, and grinned. Outside, Theodore walked home with the milk swinging in its bag, adding the whole world up in his head.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Brooke stood in front of the smoothie stand in the mall's food court with her notebook clutched like a shield. On Monday, Ms. Nasser had assigned everyone the same task: explain one economics idea out loud, in your own words, to a real audience. Brooke had drawn "supply and demand," and she had one weekend left to figure out how to say something credible about it instead of just reading a definition off her phone like Josie planned to do.

That was when she saw the strawberry cart. It was a small stand near the escalator, stacked with plastic boxes of bright red strawberries, and the line in front of it stretched past the pretzel shop. A hand-written sign said two dollars a box. Brooke got in line behind Abygaelle, who was already holding three boxes.

"I'm using these for my explanation," Brooke announced. "Strawberries cost two dollars in summer when everybody's picking them, and like five in winter. That's supply. More of something means cheaper."

"That's only half," said a voice behind her. It was the cart's owner, changing the sign. He crossed out the two and wrote four, because, he told them, he was almost sold out and wanted to stretch the last crates through closing time. "Watch the line."

Brooke watched. Within five minutes, the line had shrunk to two people. One man looked at the sign, whistled, and walked toward the pretzel shop instead. Abygaelle put one of her boxes back.

"Whoa," Brooke said, scribbling. "The price went up and people just... stopped buying."

"That's the other half," the owner said. "Price goes up, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes. No rain, no holiday, no new rival cart. Just the price."

"Nothing else changes," Brooke repeated. "So the weather can't be a variable. It's only the price doing the work."

Abygaelle squinted at her notebook. "Okay, but how do you fit this into a Monday presentation? You can't haul the whole cart into class."

"The cart can't accommodate a classroom," Brooke agreed, "but the story can." She flipped to a clean page and wrote: Step one, cheap summer strawberries, long line. Step two, raise the price, watch the line vanish. Step three, say the word.

"Which word?" Abygaelle asked.

"Demand," Brooke said, and drew a big arrow next to it. "When the price rises, demand falls. Ms. Nasser is going to think I actually understand this." She looked up at the nearly empty line and grinned. "And the best part? I watched it happen for four dollars instead of five. Smoothie?"

Abygaelle held up her last box of strawberries. "Breakfast of economists."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
story:
Isla spread her clay pieces across the kitchen table: three small bowls, a cat with one ear, and a flat plaque with her name pressed into it. She had made them all on Saturday, and now it was Tuesday, and she wanted them fired in Mr. Cardinal's kiln before Friday, when Siena was coming over to paint them together. Mr. Cardinal lived two doors down and fired things for the neighbourhood kids in exchange for cookies.

She picked up the biggest bowl and held it against her cheek. It felt cool, the way the bathroom floor felt in the morning. The cat felt cool too, but only on the bottom. She turned the plaque over and pressed her thumb into the back. Cool again, and just slightly soft, like bread that had been left out only one day.

Isla sat down and thought. The outsides were dry because the outsides were the parts the air could reach. The insides and the undersides sat against the table all night, where the air was excluded, so the damp had to be hiding there. That meant the whole piece might still be damp in the middle, where she couldn't see or feel it at all. She thought about her mother's rice pot, how the top looked done while the bottom still hissed. Hidden damp was a real thing, and it followed a pattern: thick spots and covered spots stayed wet longest.

She needed a way to test what she couldn't see. She set the big bowl upside down on the radiator in her room, where the warm air would find the hidden damp and pull it out. Then she found a scrap of mirror in her craft box, held it under the bowl for a minute, and pulled it out. A faint fog blurred the glass. Steam in the making, she thought. She put the mirror back, waited, and checked again an hour later. The fog was thinner now, like a window in monsoon season slowly clearing after the rain stops. By Thursday morning the mirror stayed clear, and the bowl felt warm all the way through, dry as a plate from the cupboard.

On Thursday after school she carried everything to Mr. Cardinal's house in a shoebox padded with an old scarf. He turned the big bowl over, tapped its base with one knuckle, and nodded. "Nice and dry," he said. "You checked it properly?" "With a mirror," Isla said. "The glass fogged up while the damp was still inside, and now it doesn't." Mr. Cardinal laughed and slid her pieces onto the kiln shelf, right beside a row of mugs. "Smart trick," he said. "I'll fire them tonight. Come by after breakfast, if Siena's ready with the paint."

activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
knowledge_domain: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
fact: In two-point perspective, vertical lines such as wall corners and door edges stay straight up and down and parallel to each other; only the horizontal edges slant toward vanishing points.
story:
Harper set her pencil down and glared at her drawing of a bedroom. The bed looked fine. The rug looked fine. But the door was the problem. No matter how carefully she drew it, the whole room seemed to be sliding toward the left corner of the paper, like the furniture was about to pour out into the hall.

"That door's going to fall on somebody," said Jiya, leaning over from the next table. "Maybe a warning sign. Beware of Tipping Door."

"It's not funny," Harper said, though she laughed anyway. "Mr. Zhao said two vanishing points, so I put every line going to one of them. Both the vanishing points are on the horizon, so all the lines slant. That's the rule." She tapped her ruler against the desk to emphasize each word.

Mr. Zhao walked past, looked at the drawing for exactly two seconds, and said, "Count your vertical lines." Then he moved on, which Harper considered deeply unhelpful.

Jiya squinted at the drawing. "You mean like the corner of the wall? Yours is leaning."

Harper went around the room and found Erin's perspective drawing, which actually looked solid. She laid Erin's page next to hers. Erin's wall corners were straight up and down. Every single one. So were her door edges. Only the horizontal edges, the ones along the tops and bottoms of walls and doors, ran slanted toward the vanishing points. In Harper's drawing, she had angled the door frame toward the right vanishing point, and that was the exact moment the room started to tip.

"Oh," Harper said. "Vertical lines stay straight. They're all parallel. Only the horizontal ones slant." She erased the leaning door frame and redrew it plumb, then checked the wall corner behind it.

Jiya held up her own page. "Is mine okay? Also, why does your door have a little ear-shaped thing on it?"

"That's the handle," Harper said. "And it's an ear, sort of. Ears are mostly cartilage, you know. Very hard to draw."

"You're so wise," Jiya said. "Wisely drawing a bedroom with no door knob."

"Handle," said Harper, and drew it round.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The phrase "according to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist.
story:
Colton slapped his card down on the kitchen table at Grandpa's house, and Kingston slapped his down half a second later. "That's my trick," they both said at once, and then they both froze, glaring across the scattered deck.

"Boys," said Grandpa from the counter, not even turning around from his coffee. "Either settle it according to Hoyle, or I take the cards back."

Kingston blinked. Colton blinked harder. "Who's Hoyle?" he asked. "The kid who owns the cards? Because these are yours."

Grandpa chuckled like that was the funniest thing he'd heard all week. "Look it up, why don't you. You've got that phone in your pocket and it isn't going to bite."

Colton dug out his phone while Kingston leaned over his shoulder. The screen glowed. They read it together, and Colton felt his eyes go wide. "It means following the rules exactly," he said. "And it comes from Edmond Hoyle. In 1742 he wrote a book that set down the rules of the card game whist." He looked at Kingston. "There was a real guy. He's been in charge of the rules for like, forever."

"So nobody here is his descendant or anything," Kingston said, "and we still have to decide who won that trick."

"Right." Colton tapped the table. Here was the real problem: no rule covered two cards hitting the table at the same time. But that was the thing to name. "Okay. The problem is we both played at once, so nobody cheated, nobody's slow. Fair rule?"

"Whoever's card is physically lower on the table wins," Kingston said, with a predatory grin that made Colton nervous, because Kingston's card was definitely on top of Colton's.

"Nope. Tie means we play it over, next hand, winner takes the whole pile." Colton held out his fist. "Deal?"

Kingston pounded it. "Deal. And when I win the pile, don't let it embarrass you."

Colton shuffled the cards back together and dealt.

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: As a teenage reporter at the Kansas City Star, Ernest Hemingway learned from a style sheet that began 'Use short sentences. Use short first paragraphs.'
story:
Riley slid her draft across the library table and groaned at it, the way you might groan at a sock that had been under the bed for a month. "Very nice," she read aloud to Samara. "The very tall man walked very slowly down the very long hall." Four verys in one sentence. Her dragon story, the one she'd been proud of yesterday, now looked like it had been stuffed with packing peanuts.

Samara leaned over. "Delete the verys. Just say tall man, long hall."

Riley tried it. The sentence shrank and, weirdly, got stronger, like it had been holding its breath and finally could exhale. "Huh," she said. "It's better with less in it. Why is it better with less in it?"

They carried the draft to Mr. Zhang at the front desk, mostly because he kept a box of trivia next to the return bin. He didn't take the paper. He reached under the desk instead and pulled out a photocopied page from a book about Ernest Hemingway. "Read the second paragraph," he said, and went back to stamping.

Riley read it, then read it again. As a teenage reporter at the Kansas City Star, Hemingway had learned from a style sheet, a single page of rules, and it began "Use short sentences. Use short first paragraphs." She held the page up. "He was a teenager? At a newspaper? And some style sheet told him that?"

"Apparently it stuck," Samara said, peeking at the page. "His paragraphs are short like yours when you're lazy."

"Mine are short like a genius's," Riley said, but she was already wondering. If the whole trick was short sentences, she could do that. She sat down, crossed out every very, every quite, every really, and rewrote a paragraph in punchy little sentences. The dragon flew. The dragon was red. The dragon was angry. She read it aloud.

It sounded like a robot doing push-ups. Even the civilian population of the library, two kids doing homework three tables away, looked up.

Samara laughed so hard she knocked over a pencil cup. "Okay, so all short is wrong too."

Riley stared at her original draft, at the photocopy, at her robot paragraph, and noticed something: the sentences that worked weren't all one length and weren't all another. They ran parallel for a while, then one broke the pattern, and that one hit hardest. "It's like a jump rope," she said slowly. "Steady, steady, steady, then the double-under." She wrote one more version, mixing them, then slid it to Samara. "Read the first line out loud."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: A proposed law is called a bill until it passes all its stages; once it becomes law it is called an Act.
story:
Jack spread his poster board across the kitchen table and stared at the word he had written in fat letters: BILL. His social studies presentation was due tomorrow, and he was stuck on something that had been bugging him since the class field trip last month.

He flashed back to that day in the legislative gallery. The tour guide had pointed to a plaque that said "An Act to Protect Wetlands," but the pamphlet in his hand called the same thing "Bill 42." He had raised his hand to ask about it, then lost his nerve when the guide moved on. Two names for one thing made no sense, and now he had to stand up in front of everyone and explain it.

Nehemiah arrived first, carrying a bag of markers, and Elias banged in behind him with a box of crackers because he always got hungry by four o'clock. They had agreed to help Jack build a game where the poster board was the legislature and a folded paper "bill" had to travel through stations. Nehemiah, who was meticulous about details, had already lettered signs for each stage in careful blue ink.

"It still doesn't work," Jack said, sliding the folded paper along the table. "The paper starts as a bill and ends as a bill. That can't be right, because the plaque at the legislature said Act."

Elias crunched a cracker and leaned over the board. "So change the sign at the end. Like a traffic sensor knows a car has passed, the last station could, you know, register that it made it through."

Jack had insisted an hour ago that the game was fine without any fancy final station, and Nehemiah had frowned at the poster ever since. Now Jack changed his mind. He tore off a strip of paper and wrote ACT in big block capitals. "A proposed law is called a bill until it passes all its stages," he said, taping the strip over the last sign. "Once it becomes law, it's called an Act."

Nehemiah's frown disappeared. He flipped the folded paper over so the blank side faced up, and Elias drew a star on it with a gold marker. Then Elias got quiet, the way he did when his mom worked late shifts, so Jack slid the whole cracker box across the table without saying anything, and Nehemiah quietly poured him a glass of milk.

There was a knock at the back door. Mr. Cruz from next door stood there holding a casserole dish, because he always cooked too much on Sundays and knew Jack's mom wouldn't be home until seven. "Smells like a project in here," he said, peering at the poster.

"Want to play the legislature?" Jack asked. "You can be the first stage."

Mr. Cruz set down the dish, rolled up his sleeves, and picked up the folded paper. "Introducing Bill 42," he announced, rapping his knuckles on the table like a gavel.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
story:
Kate spent the first ten minutes of science class not thinking about glue. She was thinking about the note in her pocket, the one she had written last night and rewritten twice. It began, "You never keep secrets. You always spill everything." It ended with a doodle of a trash can, which she'd added at eleven p.m. and now regretted.

At the next table, Shreya was testing her glue joint by hanging a stapler from it, because Mr. McKenzie had said the winning bond had to be durable enough to survive being dropped from the desktop. Shreya laughed at something Arian said, which made Kate's stomach tighten. On Friday, Kate had told Shreya that she'd made a fool of herself at the tryouts, and by Monday, Arian knew. Kate hadn't spoken to Shreya since.

While Mr. McKenzie weighed glue samples, Kate's eyes drifted to the poster taped above the sink, left over from a lesson the previous term. It said that relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like "you always" or "you never." Kate read it twice. Then she pulled out her note. "You never keep secrets" had zero specific actions in it. She crossed it out and wrote, underneath, "You told Arian what I said on Friday." It felt smaller, and also more like a thing a person could actually answer.

Shreya's stapler hit the floor with a clang that made half the class jump and made the boy next to Kate's sleeve stick to his own project, which he peeled off with a sound like tape. Arian held up her broken bond and announced, "Mine was durable for one whole second," and Mr. McKenzie said that was a record of a kind. Kate laughed despite herself, and when she looked up, Shreya was looking at her.

Kate walked over and set the note on Shreya's table. "Read the bottom part," she said. "Not the crossed-out part. Definitely not the trash can."

Shreya read it, and her face went pink. "Friday I had my vaccine appointment, remember, and then Saturday Arian asked if you were okay because you looked upset, and I panicked and said one thing. One thing, Kate. But you're right, I shouldn't have." She took out a pencil and wrote at the bottom, "I'm sorry I told her. Next time I'll say 'ask Kate.'" She held it up. "Deal?"

"That wasn't a complaint," Kate said, pointing at the crossed-out top of the page. "That was criticism. The poster says so. This version's better."

Shreya folded the note in half and tucked it under the stapler. "Then let's test the repair," she said, and hung the stapler from the glue joint again.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
story:
Leo had played "March Across the Tundra" eleven times through, start to finish, and the run at measure thirty still fell apart every single time. He lowered his trumpet and stared at the music stand as if the notes themselves were being deliberately cruel. Across the band room, Shreya sat with her flute, but she wasn't playing the whole piece. She played four measures, then the same four measures again, then again, slower, then faster.

"What are you doing?" Leo asked.

"Four measures. That's where I always miss." She didn't look up. "My cousin told me research on expert performers found that how you practice, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than playing a piece many times."

Leo wanted to argue, but he remembered last Thursday. He had played the whole march nine times and told himself that was enough, and then Ms. Sokolov had stopped the band right at his run and looked at him over her glasses until his ears burned. Nine times through, and the same stumble waited for him at measure thirty like something predatory crouched behind a snowbank, patient and sure.

So he tried it. He set the metronome slow and played only measure thirty, over and over, until his fingers could coordinate with his breath without his thinking about it. Then he added measure thirty-one. Then twenty-nine. He didn't touch the rest of the song once. It felt wrong, like cheating, like he hadn't really practiced at all.

When Ms. Sokolov called for the piece the next day, Craig leaned over before they started. "You sound nervous," Craig whispered.

"I only practiced four measures," Leo whispered back.

The band began. The melody swept along, and then measure thirty arrived, and Leo's fingers moved through the run clean and quick, every note landing where it belonged. Ms. Sokolov lowered her baton at the end and raised an eyebrow at him.

"Whatever you did," she said, "do it again Monday."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
story:
Nicholas stared at his shading project and frowned. Ms. Robinson had prescribed exactly three values for the apple drawing: light, medium, and dark, in pencil only. His dark side came out fine, but the light side looked muddy no matter how gently he pressed. Across the table, Ricardo held up two pencils that looked identical. "Watch this," he said, dragging each one across a scrap of paper. One left a soft gray stripe, the other a faint ghost of a line. "Same brand, same size. My grandpa says they're not the same inside, though."

"He wrote me a note about it," Ricardo said, pulling a folded paper from his pocket. Nicholas unfolded it and read: "Dear Ricardo, sorry I fell asleep before you left. The answer to your pencil question is in the numbers on the barrel. Look them up, and stop blaming your hand. Grandpa." Nicholas turned his own pencil over and found a small 2H near the eraser. His muddy pencil from home, the one he'd blamed all morning, said 4B.

So it was never his hand. He lined up every pencil in his tin, from a 6H to a soft 8B, and made a test strip of stripes, lightest to darkest. Then he got Ms. Robinson's approval to borrow the class set, and he and Talia tested those too, whispering over the results like scientists guarding nectar from ants. "The stripes match the numbers," Talia said. "The bigger the H, the lighter the line."

"But why?" Nicholas asked. Ricardo grinned. "Grandpa's second note." He read aloud: "The core isn't lead. It's graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks." That was it, then. The numbers were a recipe.

Nicholas redrew the light side of his apple with the 4H, so faint the paper almost looked untouched, then layered the 2H where the curve turned. Talia, who had insisted an hour ago that one pencil was plenty, was now quietly testing all twelve on her own strip, her paper a ladder of grays. Ms. Robinson leaned over Nicholas's shoulder. "This one goes on the wall," she said. "I was worried about that light side, honestly. It looked a little vulnerable back there." Nicholas laughed and picked up the 4H again.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
story:
Jade plucked the low E string on her guitar and listened to it grumble like a sleepy bear. That was the sound she wanted for the song she was writing, but the song needed the same bear sound, only higher, and she could not find it anywhere on the neck.

"Try fret five," said Zakaria, who was waiting on the studio couch for his own lesson. "Fret five is always right."

"Fret five is right for your violin, maybe," Jade said. She pressed the string at the fifth fret and plucked. Wrong bear. She tried seven. Wrong, wronger bear.

Mr. Barrett looked up from tuning a ukulele. "You have ten minutes before your lesson starts, Jade. Use them."

She slid her finger up the neck, testing each fret like she was checking doorknobs for a hidden room. At the twelfth fret, right where the neck met the body, she noticed something odd. There were two little dots inlaid there, like tiny eyes watching her.

She pressed the string down exactly on that spot and plucked.

The same bear. The exact same note, just higher, as if the bear had stood up on a stool. She plucked the open string, then the twelfth fret, back and forth, back and forth, grinning so hard her cheeks hurt.

"Zakaria. Zakaria, listen." She played the pair of notes three times. "Same note, higher. I pressed the string at the exact middle of it. The twelfth fret is the middle of the string."

Zakaria came over and bent close, squinting at the neck. "That can't be a coincidence," he said. "Half the string, and the note jumps up one octave."

"That's the word," Jade said. "Octave. My mom sings that word at me all the time."

Renaud barged in with his trumpet case, nearly dropping it on Zakaria's foot. "What are we yelling about?"

"Bears," said Zakaria. "Musical bears."

Jade was already testing the idea, because an idea was only a rumor until you tested it. She measured with her eyes: the twelfth fret sat halfway between the nut and the bridge, where the string ended. She moved her finger a tiny bit off the middle and plucked. The note wobbled away from the clean bear sound, sour and wobbly. Back to the exact middle: the clean octave returned. Middle, half, octave. It worked on the A string too, and the high E, agile little notes leaping up like frogs.

"I could write the whole chorus now," she said. "Low bear, high bear, low bear."

"Please don't abandon the bear idea before your lesson," Zakaria said. "I want to hear it from the waiting room."

Mr. Barrett set down the ukulele. "Jade, you just skipped three weeks of my curriculum on your own. What did you find?"

She held up the guitar, pointed at the two little dots, and said, "Your guitar has been keeping a secret right in the middle of the neck."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
story:
The itch started in the third inning, somewhere deep under the plaster on Tyler's left arm, right where he couldn't reach. He was keeping score for Ms. Xu's gym class while his broken arm healed, sitting in the grass by the soccer field with a clipboard on his knee, and the itch grew until it was all he could think about.

"Stop wiggling," said Ivan, who was sitting beside him. "You're making the score all crooked."

"I can't help it. It itches." Tyler picked up a ruler from the clipboard, slid it toward the opening near his elbow, and then stopped. He remembered the doctor's exact words from the day the cast went on: don't slide pencils or sticks inside to scratch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining. He put the ruler down.

"Then what are you going to do?" asked Brendan, jogging over from the field during a water break. "You look like a dog with fleas."

Tyler stared at the cast. If he couldn't touch the itch, maybe he could fool it. He pressed his fingertip against the outside of the plaster and rubbed small circles, right above the itchy spot. The pressure traveled through, and the itch faded.

"That," Ivan said, "is the weirdest phenomenon I've ever seen."

"It's not a phenomenon. It's just pressure." But Tyler was grinning. He'd tested an idea, and it worked, and he hadn't wrecked the lining the doctor had warned him about.

Ms. Xu came by after the game. "You conquered that score sheet," she said, tapping the clipboard. "Robust work, Tyler."

"Ms. Xu, if someone else breaks an arm, can I tell them the trick?"

"Tell me first," she said, and pulled a thin balloon pump from her equipment bag. "Cool air from one of these works too. Want to borrow it Monday?"

Tyler held the pump up like a trophy. "Deal."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest, begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday.
story:
Laurence had been at Elie's house since four o'clock, and so far the plan was going perfectly. They had built a blanket fort in the living room, eaten half a bowl of popcorn, and agreed that Kiaan's opinion about the best soccer team was completely biased since he only liked them because his uncle worked there. Then Elie's mom came through with a basket and started collecting phones, tablets, and even the TV remote.

"Whoa," Laurence said, holding her phone against her chest. "Why?"

"It's almost sunset on Friday," Elie said, like that answered everything. "Shabbat starts at sunset tonight, so the screens go away." She dropped her own phone in the basket without complaining, which somehow made it worse.

Laurence followed Elie's mom into the kitchen, determined to intervene on behalf of the popcorn movie they had planned. "How long does this last? An hour?"

"Until tomorrow after nightfall," Elie's mom said, sliding a tray of challah into the oven. "Then we get everything back."

Laurence did the math in her head. Sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday. That was more than a whole day without her phone. She wanted to argue, but the bread smelled so good that she lost her place. Also, she noticed, nobody in the kitchen looked like they were being punished. Elie's dad was setting the table and humming, and Elie was already dragging two chairs together for the fort kids.

At dinner, Laurence tried an experiment. "So we just... talk?"

"And sing, and play cards, and argue about soccer," Elie said, dealing a hand on the cleared table. "Kiaan would say you're biased against resting."

"Maybe I am," Laurence said. She picked up her cards and, for the first time all week, did not check the time once. Outside the window, the sky finally went dark. "Okay. Deal me in again."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Salt melts ice by lowering the temperature at which water freezes, but ordinary rock salt stops working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius (14 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
The thermometer on the back fence read minus twelve Celsius, and Brayden stared at it like it had lied to him. Yesterday his dad had scattered rock salt all over the back steps and the paved path beside the shed, and the ice had gone slushy within an hour. Today the same salt sat on top of the same ice, gray and crunchy, melting absolutely nothing.

"Are you going to stand there all morning?" Macy called from the middle of the yard, where she was packing snow blocks into a wall. She had been planning this fort since the first flakes fell, and she needed the pathway cleared so her little brother could drag the sled through. "Because I need that path open by noon."

"I'm thinking," Brayden said. He crouched and pressed his mitten onto the salted ice. Solid. Yesterday, in almost the same spot, the salt had chewed right through. The only thing different was the cold itself. He tried to digest that idea, turning it over the way he turned over a puzzle in math class. Maybe salt didn't melt ice just because salt was salt. Maybe it lowered the temperature at which water freezes, and that only helped if the air wasn't colder than the new, lower point.

He found his dad's thermometer, the pointy one for meat, and stuck it into a snowbank. Minus twelve. He remembered the line on the salt bag in the garage: works down to about minus 10 Celsius, 14 Fahrenheit. He did the subtraction twice. Twelve was colder than ten, so the salt had quit.

"It's too cold for the salt to work," he announced. "Below about minus 10 Celsius, 14 Fahrenheit, rock salt just gives up. So we do it the old way." He grabbed the metal shovel and swung at the path, and the ice cracked off in satisfying plates.

Macy gave an eloquent nod toward the sled trail, then went back to her wall. "Laser focus, Brayden. Keep swinging."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: A callback closing returns to the opening hook at the end, which makes a speech feel complete.
story:
Ryan stood on the auditorium stage for the fourth time that afternoon, holding his note cards, and stopped at the end of his speech the way a bike stops when the chain falls off. "And, um. That's it," he said. The words dropped into the empty seats and lay there.

Ms. Whitaker called from the third row, "Your opening was excellent. The hook about your grandmother's parrot escaping at Thanksgiving had everyone listening. Three strong points. Now you need an ending."

"That's what Troy said," Ryan answered. "I just can't find one." He looked at his cards. Point one, point two, point three, and then a blank card he had been staring at for two days.

He sat on the edge of the stage and checked his phone. Alexe had texted him twenty minutes ago: "Couldn't sleep on your problem, so here's a thought. What if the ending doesn't come after your three points? What if it's already at the beginning? Go back to your first line. That's where the ending hides. Try it and report back."

Ryan read the message twice. His first line was about the parrot landing on the principal's head mid-Thanksgiving-dinner because his grandmother taught it one phrase: "Speech, please." He had been so busy prioritizing his three points that he hadn't looked at the opening again. He walked to center stage, ran through the whole speech, and when he reached the blank card, he said, "So the next time my grandmother's parrot lands on someone's head, we'll all know what to say. Speech, please."

It landed. He could feel it land, the way the whole thing clicked shut like a lid.

Troy, running lines backstage, poked his head out. "A callback closing," he said. "It returns to the hook. I didn't think you'd figure that out before the assembly tomorrow."

"I didn't," Ryan said, waving his phone. "Alexe did. I owe her a milkshake." He squared his blank card one last time, then flipped it over and wrote on the back: parrot returns.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Zoe stood at the boards watching the shooter tutor blink its numbers while Eunice taped her stick. Yesterday the local sports site had posted two headlines about Zoe's team, and Zoe had screenshot both: "Vipers jump 10 percentage points" and "Vipers see 25 percent rise." Ten and twenty-five. Same team, same week. She couldn't make them match, and it bothered her like a pebble in her skate boot.

"My shooting percentage," Zoe said, pulling out her phone. "It was 40 percent, and now it's 50 percent." She flicked a puck toward the empty net and missed wide. "One story says that's a rise of 10 percentage points, and the other says it's a 25 percent increase, and I think one of them has to be wrong."

Eunice skated over, breath fogging. "My dad says that all the time about polls. He goes, ten percentage points and 25 percent, same thing." She dug a puck out of the corner and passed it hard to Zoe's tape. "Want me to keep feeding you until it makes sense?"

So Zoe tested it, because a headline felt different from proof. Fifty shots, and she counted every single one, marking them on a whiteboard Mr. Tehrani kept by the bench for drills. Forty percent meant twenty in, and she knew that much cold. Fifty percent meant twenty-five in, which was five more, and five was exactly a quarter of twenty. She said it out loud, just to hear it in the cold air: "Five more out of twenty. That's a quarter. Twenty-five percent." The two numbers hadn't been fighting each other at all; they were two doors into the same room. She almost dropped her marker.

Mr. Tehrani leaned over the boards on his way to the Zamboni tunnel. "Board looks busy, Zoe."

"It's my percentages," she said. "They finally line up." She snapped the cap back on the marker, and Eunice fired another pass, and Zoe one-timed it off the post and in.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wind makes cold air feel colder because it carries heat away from the skin faster, which is what the wind chill number describes.
story:
The snow day announcement came at six forty in the morning, and by seven, Felix was already planning the greatest fort in the history of his street. Gaelle and Felix-Antoine had texted that they'd come by at noon, which gave him four hours to build something worth crawling into. He'd promised them walls, a roof, and a secret back entrance, and he intended to preserve that promise even if his fingers fell off.

Outside, the air bit harder than it should have. He'd seen minus eight on the weather app, which felt unpleasant but survivable, yet his cheeks stung like he'd stuck them in a freezer. He pulled out the phone again and scrolled down. There it was: wind chill, minus nineteen. The wind chill was far colder than the actual temperature, and somehow that number, not the real one, was what his face believed.

"That's crazy," he muttered, and decided to test it. He scooped a shovelful of snow and stood in the open middle of the street, holding one bare hand out for a slow count of ten. Then he walked to the spot behind Mrs. Fontaine's hedge, where the wind couldn't reach, and did the same thing with the other hand. The difference was enormous. Behind the hedge, his hand just felt cold. In the street, it felt like it was being robbed. The wind, he realized, was carrying heat away from his skin faster than the still air was, which had to be why the wind chill number existed at all.

"Wind chill," he announced to an imaginary audience, "minus nineteen, and I have the evidence." His audience turned out to be real. Ms. Desir, the neighbour two doors down, was scraping her windshield and laughing at him. "Talking to your hands now, Felix?" she called. "Only when they're the smartest ones outside," he said, and she laughed so hard she dropped her ice scraper.

He rebuilt the whole plan in five minutes. The fort would go behind the hedge row, tucked out of the wind, with the opening facing away from the gusts that kept shoving snow down his collar. He'd already wasted forty minutes shivering in the open, and noon was coming fast, so he shovelled like his snow reputation depended on it, because with Gaelle and Felix-Antoine, bragging rights were the only currency that mattered. When the two of them trudged up the street at eleven fifty, Felix-Antoine's scarf frozen stiff on one side, Felix stood proudly at his hedge-sheltered entrance. "Welcome to the warmest fort on the street," he said. "Well," Gaelle said, ducking inside, "the least frozen one, anyway."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
story:
Penelope lay on her bed with a box of tissues and stared at the ceiling, where a water stain spread like a map of nowhere. Two days ago her nose had been a monsoon, unstoppable, and her whole body had ached like she had run a mile carrying a backpack full of bricks. Today the flood had dried up. Her throat felt arid but not sore, and her temperature had read normal twice in a row. She hypothesized that a normal temperature meant the flu was gone, which meant she could go to Leana's birthday party tonight, which meant she would not miss the ice cream cake.

She texted Conrad to tell him the plan. His reply came fast: "Day two? My mom made me stay home the whole week when I had it in November. She said something about the first three days being the worst for spreading it. Look it up."

Penelope scowled at her phone. She opened the browser and typed. The CDC page loaded slowly, and she read it twice to be sure. According to the CDC, people with the flu were most contagious during the first three days of their illness. Today was day two. She checked her own reasoning against it, and it held: feeling better did not mean the third day had come and gone.

She flopped back against her pillow and groaned. Tomorrow was day three, and the party was tonight. "Of course it is," she said out loud.

Then she sat up, typed a message to Leana, and sent it before she could change her mind. "I can't come tonight because I'm still on the contagious clock. Save me a corner of cake. Saturday, I will come over myself and bring your present." While she waited, she propped the phone against the tissue box and started a video call with Conrad. His face appeared, headphones on, homework spread around him.

"Trivia night?" he asked.

"Trivia night," she said, and pulled her blanket over her legs.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: In Google, the word OR between two search words must be typed in capital letters to find pages containing either word.
story:
Katherine had a project due Monday about which pet was easier to train, and she was stuck at Tanya's kitchen table with a laptop and a bag of cheese crackers. She typed cats or dogs into the search bar and hit enter. The results were terrible. There were pages about "Cats for Adoption," a shopping site selling dog beds, and three listings with the word "Sponsored" tucked in tiny print at the top.

"Those are ads," Tanya said, leaning over her shoulder. "My mom clicks on them by accident all the time and then we get coupons for dog food for a month. It's a real consequence."

"I want actual pages," Katherine said. She scrolled past the sponsored listings and found one article about cats and nothing about dogs at all. She stared at the search bar like it had betrayed her personally. "It ignored my 'or.' It's only giving me cats."

Tanya shrugged and stole a cracker. "Maybe it doesn't like dogs."

Katherine frowned. She opened a new tab and tried cats OR dogs, typing the word in capital letters just to see what would happen, because once she'd read that capital letters sometimes mattered to computers. The page loaded. Suddenly there were pages about dogs, pages about cats, pages about both. She sat back so fast she nearly knocked over the crackers.

"It worked! The OR has to be capital letters or it doesn't count." She tried lowercase again to verify, and got the sad cats-only results again. Capital letters, and the dogs came back. It was like a secret password.

"Prove it," Tanya said, so Katherine showed her both searches side by side. Tanya squinted at the screens, then nodded. "Unanimous. The capital letters win."

"You're one person. You can't be unanimous."

"I'm unanimous with the laptop," Tanya said. "We voted together."

Katherine laughed and went back to work. She found three real articles about pet training, skipped past the sponsored dog-bed listings, and wrote her first paragraph. At the top of her notes she typed, in careful capitals, REMEMBER: OR. Tanya read it upside down and raised her cracker like a toast.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
story:
Ariana climbed the synagogue basement stairs behind her mother, carrying a plate of matzah wrapped in foil. The Passover Seder would start in an hour, and long tables already stretched across the hall, set with candles and cups of wine and one shiny silver cup nobody was allowed to drink from. Her little cousin Danny had been practicing the Four Questions all week. At the Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks them, and Danny, age seven, was the youngest, so the job was his.

Except Danny looked green. He sat in the corner hugging his Haggadah like a life raft. "What if I forget question three?" he whispered when Ariana sat down beside him. She had offered to tutor him on Tuesday, walking him through each question twice, but his voice had gotten smaller every time they practiced.

"I'll be right across the table," she said.

Danny's chin trembled. "Baby Micah is asleep in the stroller. If he wakes up before me, he's the youngest and I'm off the hook." Ariana laughed, then stopped, because he was serious.

The Seder began. Mr. Nur, the rabbi, blessed the wine, and everyone drank. Then he raised his hand for silence, and all eyes turned to Danny. Danny stood up. His mouth opened. Nothing came out. The silence stretched so long that Ariana could hear the clock on the wall.

She looked at sleeping Micah, then at Danny, and did the math. If a baby too small to talk couldn't ask, then Danny was still the youngest able child, and there was no escaping it. So the only way out was through. She caught his eye, held up four fingers, and mouthed the first words, slowly, the way a ferry carries people across water, one passenger at a time.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?" Danny said, barely a squeak. Ariana mouthed the next line. He took a breath and gave it again, louder. By the fourth question his voice filled the whole basement, and when he finished, Mr. Nur said, "Excellent," and the tables broke into applause.

After the meal, while the plagues were being recited and everyone dripped wine onto their plates, Danny slid into the seat beside Ariana. "Next year," he said, "maybe I could get someone prestigious to tutor me. Like you."

Ariana grinned and stole one of his matzah balls. "Deal," she said.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
story:
The end-of-season party was supposed to be fun, but halfway through the pizza, Katherine noticed that nobody was laughing anymore. Finnley kept spinning a basketball on one finger without looking up, and Hassan had gone quiet in the corner, folding his jersey into smaller and smaller squares. Katherine understood why, even if she couldn't quite name it: in two weeks the team would be sorted onto new rosters, and this exact group would never play together again. The feeling had been eroding the whole party, quietly, like water wearing down a step.

In the gym office, borrowing tape from Ms. Khan's desk, Katherine spotted an old college textbook lying open. A diagram showed groups moving through stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, and one more, added later. She read the caption twice, then carried the book back out onto the court.

"Hassan. Finnley. Look at this." She set the book on the bleachers between them. "In 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, because groups weren't done after performing." She tapped the last box. "It's called adjourning. It's when a group finishes its work and breaks up." Finnley stopped spinning the ball. "So the sad part is a real stage? Like, someone studied it?" "Somebody thought it mattered enough to add," Katherine said.

Hassan unfolded his jersey and smoothed it flat. From that perspective, the strange mood wasn't a failure of the party; it was the team doing its last piece of work together. Katherine grabbed the marker board from the score table and wrote ADJOURNING in tall letters, then underneath, every player's name in a column.

"Contemporary teams do a wall," she announced, not entirely sure that was true but deciding it should be. "Everybody signs, everybody writes one thing they'll remember." Finnley grabbed the marker first and printed Katherine's behind-the-back pass from the Millbrook game. By the time Ms. Khan peeked in to say the building was closing, the board was full, and Hassan was taking a photo of it, the flash bouncing off the trophy case.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
story:
Mila sat at the kitchen table with her recorder notes spread in front of her, but her eyes kept drifting to the piano in the corner. The passage in "The Silver Stream" would not cooperate. Her fingers knew where to go, yet every time she reached the sixth bar, they tangled like kite string in wind. She had practiced it eleven times after school, and the eleventh was worse than the first.

Celeste had watched part of it through the window while raking leaves next door, and she had come over afterward with her gloves still on. "You played that same bit over and over," Celeste said. "My mom says that's how you learn, repetition."

"Then it's broken," Mila said. "I repeat and it gets worse."

Mr. Sow, who lived across the street and tuned pianos for a living, had told her something once that she kept turning over. It was last spring, when he was adjusting the sticky pedal on their old upright. "There was a study where people practiced a sequence of finger movements," he had said, tightening a screw while the strings hummed like a tiny turbine inside the case. "A night of sleep after the practice improved their performance the next day, without any extra practice." He had said it offhand, the way he mentioned the weather, and then he had packed his tools and gone home.

Mila had dismissed it then. It sounded like a trick, like the synthetic maple syrup her grandfather preferred over the real kind: cheaper, but it didn't do the job. You couldn't get better at something by sleeping. Except tonight, standing at the piano with aching knuckles, she wanted to test it. It was a simple idea. Practice the passage until her fingers had the shape of it, even a rough shape, then sleep, then play it once in the morning before touching it again.

She worked through the passage five more times, slowly, until she could feel the pattern rather than fight it. Then she closed the keyboard lid, ate dinner, and went to bed early, telling her mother she wanted to be rested for once.

In the morning, the kitchen smelled like toast, and pale light came through the curtains onto the piano keys. Mila lifted the lid, set her fingers on the sixth bar, and played it through. Her hands moved cleanly, one note after another, as if the pattern had been transmitted to them overnight through some wire she couldn't see. She played the whole passage twice more, and both times it held.

At school she found Celeste by the lockers. "It worked," Mila said. "I couldn't play it last night, and this morning it was just there."

Celeste frowned. "You didn't practice more?"

"Not one extra minute. Sleep did it."

That afternoon, Mila set the sheet music on the rack and opened to the next page, where the notes ran uphill in a long bright climb.

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: Bharatanatyam, a classical dance from Tamil Nadu in India, uses symbolic hand gestures called mudras that work like words to tell a story.
story:
Easton's socks slid on the kitchen tile as he spun, and he grabbed the counter to keep from crashing into the toaster. In two weeks he was supposed to perform a Bharatanatyam dance at the community festival, and so far he could do the steps but not the hands. His grandmother had taught him the sequence over video calls from Chennai, and each hand shape had to be exact.

Calista sat on a stool eating crackers, watching him attempt the same eight counts for the fifth time. "Your hands are doing something different each time," she said. "It matters, doesn't it? You keep saying it matters."

"It matters because of mudras," Easton said, shaking out his fingers. "They're symbolic hand gestures that work like words to tell a story."

"Words? So if you mix them up..."

He froze mid-gesture, one palm flat, the other raised. "Then I change the story." He tried the next phrase, the one where his grandmother had shown a hand tilting like a lotus blooming. Instead his thumb crossed wrong and his fingers hooked into something that looked more like a claw. Calista burst out laughing so hard a cracker crumb went down the wrong pipe, and she wheezed, "You just told the whole audience you have a rebellious intestine."

"That is not what that gesture says." But Easton couldn't prove it, which embarrassed him, because he realized he'd been rehearsing the dance like a pattern of feet and never checked whether his hands were actually saying anything. His grandmother had described each mudra over the phone, but he'd watched her feet more than her fingers. He grabbed his phone and called her, and she answered mid-breakfast, holding her hands up to the camera so he could copy each shape slowly, lotus by lotus, word by word.

A knock came at the kitchen door, and Ms. Pérez from next door leaned in, flour on her apron. "I could hear thumping. Is this a rehearsal or a wrestling match?"

"It's a story," Easton said, palms folding into the first mudra, "about a lotus."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Overmixing muffin batter develops gluten in the flour, which makes muffins tough and can leave long tunnels inside them.
story:
The recipe card in Grandma's tin box said "Blueberry Muffins" in faded ink, and at the bottom, underlined twice, it read, "Stir only until the dry disappears. Overmixing develops the gluten in the flour. Tough muffins, long tunnels inside." Kayla read it three times. How could stirring too much change what was inside a muffin? You couldn't see gluten, couldn't feel it happening. She decided to test it, the way her science teacher would want.

"You're making two batches?" Luna asked, peering over Kayla's shoulder at the mixing bowls. "One for science, one for eating," Kayla said. "Batch A gets stirred just until the flour vanishes, lumps and all. Batch B gets stirred until it's perfectly smooth, like cake batter." Grandma was out in the garden, and the girls had the kitchen to themselves. Kayla turned the dial to three hundred fifty degrees and slid the racks into place while the oven preheated, because the card said the oven had to be ready first. The pantry looked impoverished after their raid, one bag of flour left and half a carton of blueberries, so they split everything carefully between the two bowls.
