The batters looked different before they even baked. Batch A was lumpy and shaggy, and Batch B sat glossy and smooth. "The smooth one has to win," Luna said. "It looks nicer." Kayla wasn't sure. She'd stirred Batch B a long time, and the more she stirred, the stretchier and stringier it got, like it was turning into something else entirely.

Twenty-two minutes later, they pulled both trays out and split the muffins open while they were still warm. The lumpy-batter muffins were tender, with an even, bumpy crumb. The smooth-batter muffins were chewy, and when Kayla held half up to the window light, she could see long, narrow tunnels running through the middle like worm trails. "Tunnels," she said. "The card was right." She pulled out a pencil, crossed out nothing on the recipe, but wrote at the top of her notebook, "Revise hypothesis: lumpy batter wins." Grandma came in with dirt on her hands, sniffed the air, and asked, "Which one do I get?" Kayla handed her a lumpy one and said, "Trust me."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
Christopher had been sure he would win the school spelling bee until the word "bite" knocked Jaden out in the practice round. "B-I-T-E," Jaden had said, scowling at the silent e on the whiteboard. "Why is there an e if nobody says it?" Nobody had an answer, and that was the problem. The bee was in three days, and Christopher knew that half the tricky words had the same weird ghost letters. If he couldn't see the pattern behind them, he was guessing.

At the library he pulled a dusty book about the history of English off the bottom shelf, and tucked inside it he found a note in looping handwriting, signed by someone who had clearly studied the same thing. The note said: "It's called the Great Vowel Shift. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation." Christopher read it four times. So the letters weren't lying, exactly. They were frozen in time, and the sounds had moved out from under them. It felt radical, like discovering the gym floor had been built on a different map. He copied the note onto an index card and tested a simple idea: any word with a vowel that looked wrong might be a very old word, wearing its original spelling.

The day of the bee, the gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn from the concession table. Ms. Pritchard stood at the microphone, and rows of folding chairs held half the school. Katerina sat on Christopher's left, bouncing her knee so hard her chair squeaked. "I didn't sleep," she whispered. He tore a strip off his program and wrote on it: "Old words keep weird spellings. It's not you, it's history." She read it, laughed once, and her knee went still. His own nervousness tried to invade his stomach anyway, but he kept his index card in his pocket like currency he could spend whenever a word looked impossible.

Round four took out Jaden on "neighbor," and Katerina survived "knife" by closing her eyes and slowing way down. Then it was just the two of them. Ms. Pritchard cleared her throat. "Christopher. Your word is 'sweet.'"

He could hear the double e perfectly, but his brain flashed on bite, on knife, on all those ghost letters. His idea said: check whether this is a word where the sound shifted. He said it slowly, "S-W-E-E-T," and paused, listening for anything hiding at the end. Nothing. Some words were exactly what they seemed.

"That is correct," Ms. Pritchard said, and the gym burst into clapping. Katerina hugged him so hard she knocked the index card out of his pocket, and Jaden lunged for it, held it up, and shouted, "The Great Vowel Shift!"

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Fire-safety guidance says to put out a campfire by drowning it with water, stirring the ashes, and drowning it again until everything is cool to the touch.
story:
Keira slid into the booth at the roadside diner and pressed her palms against the cold formica, which felt wonderful after two hours in a hot car. Her family had camped at Pine Hollow last night, and this morning they had driven away in a rush because her little brother had tripped on the fire pit's stone ring and bopped his head. Their mom had spent twenty minutes checking his eyes and asking him questions, convinced he might have a concussion, though by the time they reached the diner he was loudly demanding pancakes.

That was when Keira started thinking instead of eating her toast. Dad had thrown one bucket of water on the campfire before they left, and the pit had hissed and steamed and then sat there looking harmless. But her brother had touched a stone beside it, and the stone had been warm. Warm enough to matter. She kept turning it over in her mind: water had gone on once, the top layer of ash had gone gray, but underneath, where she could not see, could coals still be alive? Fire hidden under ash would not be visible. There would be no way to know except to test the surface and dig.

She borrowed the waitress's pen and drew a circle on her napkin, then a line through the ash like a cross section. "Frederick would say I'm being gullible, believing a fire can hide," she muttered, thinking of her classmate who doubted everything except his own opinions. But this was the opposite of gullible. It was doubting the obvious.

"Can I use your phone?" she asked her dad. He handed it over, still monitoring her brother's yawns. Keira searched how to put out a campfire, and there it was: drown it with water, stir the ashes, then drown it again, and keep going until everything is cool to the touch. Twice. Plus stirring, to open up the hidden middle. That was the part they had skipped.

"Pine Hollow is eleven miles back," she said, sliding the phone across the table. "We have to return. We poured water once and didn't stir anything, and the stones were still warm. If wind gets into buried coals, the whole hollow could burn." Her dad looked at the napkin drawing, then at the phone, then at her. He stood, dropped a twenty on the table, and told her brother he could eat his pancakes in the car.

They reached the campsite in fifteen minutes. Keira fetched the bucket from the trunk, dumped water on the pit, and stirred the ash with a stick until black coals rose up from under the gray, still whispering heat. She drowned it again, stirred again, and kept at it while her dad held her jacket out of the smoke. Finally she knelt and laid the back of her hand against a chunk of charred wood, then a stone, then the far edge of the pit.

"Cold," she said. "All of it. Touch it."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
story:
Clara set her plate of rice down on the long table and then noticed that her grandmother's plate held only fruit, milk, and a few fried potatoes made without the usual batter. This was the third time this month that Grandma had skipped rice at a family dinner, and Clara wanted to know why.

"Why aren't you eating rice?" she asked, sitting down beside her.

Grandma smiled. "It is called Ekadashi," she said. "The eleventh day of each half of the lunar month."

Clara counted on her fingers under the table. The lunar month split into two halves, so the eleventh day came around twice, not once. That explained why it kept happening. But it didn't explain the rice, so she decided to test an idea. She carried her plate down the table like a waiter transporting dishes at a restaurant and asked her uncle, who was also fasting today, whether he would take some bread.

"No grains today," he said, "and no beans either. It is a day for Vishnu."

Clara walked back along the median strip of tablecloth between the two long rows of dishes, thinking. Grandma skipped rice twice a month, but only on those particular days, never on other days, even ordinary ones when she wasn't very hungry. So it wasn't about appetite. It was about the day itself, and about grains and beans, which meant her uncle's "no grains" matched Grandma's missing rice. Two fasters, one rule.

"It's a pattern," Clara told her cousin Francesco, who was building a robust tower of puris on his plate. "The day of the month tells you what's on their plates. Twice every month."

Francesco looked down the table. "So next time Grandma passes the rice, we can check the calendar first."

Clara picked up a banana from the fruit bowl and set it on Grandma's plate, next to the milk.

"For Vishnu," she said.

Grandma took her hand and squeezed it, and the two of them watched the moon rise over the garden while the rest of the family went back for seconds.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
story:
The hospital corridor smelled like soap and coffee, and Aaron had until 8:00, when the nurses said visiting hours ended and the room would be cleared for good. That was the deadline that mattered. His grandfather lay in the bed by the window, looking smaller than Aaron had ever seen him, frail in a way that seemed wrong for a man who used to carry two full grocery bags up three flights of stairs. Aaron stood in the doorway, hands in his pockets, unable to make his feet move.

In the waiting room down the hall, his friend Oscar had shown him a video on his phone, some cat walking into a sliding glass door, and Aaron had laughed. Actually laughed, out loud, the same day his grandfather died. He kept thinking about it now, turning it over. If he could laugh, maybe he hadn't really loved his grandfather enough. Maybe something in him was broken. He searched the family lounge for evidence either way, and on the rack of pamphlets beside the coffee machine he found one about grief. On page three it described a dual process model from 1999, worked out by researchers named Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, and it said grieving people move back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. Not one then the other. Both, alternating, like tides.

Aaron read it twice. Then he decided to test it, right there, because that was the kind of thing Grandpa would have done. He let himself watch Oscar's video again and the laugh came, easy and real. Then he looked at the doorway of the room and the loss rushed in like cold water, and his eyes burned. Then Alessia arrived with her mom and asked what the pamphlet said, and while he explained about the back and forth, he caught himself grinning at a memory of Grandpa arguing with a parking meter. It was true. He swung between the two, over and over, and nobody could enforce a rule that said he had to stay on one side.

At 7:51 Ms. Shevchenko, the neighbour from 4B who had known Grandpa for thirty years, came down the hall carrying his old crossword book. She squeezed Aaron's shoulder and said the service tomorrow would need someone with a strong constitution to read the poem, and asked if he was up for it. Aaron wiped his eyes, took the book, and walked into the room before the clock could stop him. He leaned close to his grandfather's ear and whispered, "Twelve across. Seven letters. Starts with C."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: If an 'if touching' block inside a forever loop adds a point and nothing moves the sprites apart, the score keeps rising for as long as they touch.
story:
Ivy dragged her laptop to the table where Hillary was already untangling a nest of wires. The gym smelled like floor wax and pizza, because the robotics competition shared the building with a food fair, and somebody's sampler tray of international cuisine had gone two tables over. Their Scratch game was due on the projector in twenty minutes.

"Watch this," Ivy said. She clicked the green flag. In the game, a cat chased a mouse around a kitchen, and whenever the cat touched a golden coin, the score was supposed to go up by one. Instead, the score read 200 and was still climbing.

Hillary leaned in. "The coin's worth two hundred points? We never made it worth two hundred."

"We made it worth one," Ivy said. She stopped the program and opened the script. The score block sat inside a forever loop, right next to an if touching coin block. She put her finger on the screen. "It adds a point every time it goes around. And the coin never disappears, so they just keep touching."

"So it adds a point forever," Hillary said.

"That's my guess. But I want to test it." Ivy moved the cat sprite away from the coin with her mouse, and the score froze at 647. She moved it back. The number began to climb again, one point at a time, as fast as the loop could run. She nudged the cat off the coin once more and the number stopped.

"Add a hide block," Hillary said. "Make the coin disappear."

Ivy had been about to delete the whole forever loop and start over. She paused with her hand on the trackpad. "You're right. The loop is fine. The coin is the problem." She dropped a hide block under the score block and ran the game again. This time the cat touched the coin, the score ticked up exactly one, and the coin vanished.

Mr. Kaminski walked past their table and looked at the screen. "That looks competent," he said. "You two are on in five."

At the projector, the judges asked Ivy to recount how she had found the bug. "The score told me something I couldn't see," she said, and clicked the green flag. The cat caught the coin, the coin vanished, and the score read one.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number makes an equivalent fraction, so one quarter equals three twelfths.
story:
The fractions on the board looked like a locked door. Mr. Popescu had written one half plus one quarter, and then, worse, one half minus one twelfth, and Brooke's pencil hovered without moving. Around her, Adelina was already writing fast, and Hassan kept glancing at the clock like the bell might save him. Brooke had missed two days with the flu, and everyone else had learned something she hadn't. She could speculate all she wanted about what it was, but guessing wouldn't fill her paper.

She tried one half minus one twelfth anyway. One of something minus one of something else. She wrote an answer, crossed it out, and wrote a different one. Then the classroom door opened and Mr. Popescu announced a surprise check quiz, five problems, collected at the end of class. Brooke's stomach dropped. Two of the five problems had unlike denominators, staring up at her like traps.

She put her pencil down and let her mind drift back to Saturday, when she and Adelina and Hassan had ordered a pizza at the shop near the rink. The man behind the counter had cut Adelina's quarter into three thinner slices because she asked for it that way, and Brooke remembered exactly what happened next. Hassan had reached for one of the thin slices, and Adelina had said, "Hey, those three are still my quarter." They had slid the three small pieces together on the tray and checked. The three twelfths covered the same space as the one big quarter. Nobody had explained it. They had just seen it, right there between the napkin dispenser and the parmesan shakers.

Back in the classroom, Brooke picked up her pencil again. If one quarter and three twelfths covered the same space, then multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number must make an equivalent fraction. She tested it on her quiz paper, quietly, in the margin. One quarter times three on the top and three on the bottom gave three twelfths. The same amount, just cut smaller. She tried it again with one half, multiplying top and bottom by six, and got six twelfths. Now the subtraction problem made sense: six twelfths minus one twelfth was five twelfths. Her hand moved fast through the rest of the quiz, and there was a strange irony in it, that being sick and missing the lesson might have helped her, because she had figured the rule out herself instead of just copying notes.

When Mr. Popescu walked the rows collecting papers, he paused at Brooke's desk longer than at the others. She held her breath. He looked at the margin where she had tested her idea, the little pizza slices of numbers, and one corner of his mouth lifted.

"Saturday homework?" he asked.

"Pizza," Brooke whispered.

He tapped her paper once with his finger, the top problem, the one she had been most unsure of, and kept walking. At his desk he sorted the stack, and Brooke watched, waiting, until he set her paper on the right side of the pile.

Adelina leaned over. "Which side is which?"

Brooke grinned and slid down in her chair. "Guess."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens.
story:
At the edge of the quarry, Maya spread her rock collection on a flat stone: nine rocks she and her friends had gathered that morning. Mr. Esposito's contest started at four o'clock, and the rule was simple: sort every rock as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic, and explain your reasoning. Scarlett leaned over the pile, holding up a gray rock freckled with pale specks. "This one has to be sedimentary," she said. "It looks like somebody glued sand together."

Maya took the speckled rock and turned it in the light. She had sorted six already. The sandstone was easy, because its layers looked like a stack of pancakes, and the limestone had a shell pressed into it, which meant it had formed from things that settle and harden over time. She'd even found a rock with a curled larva fossil, a creature that had died and been buried before it could become anything else. But the speckled rock didn't have layers or shells. "Sand doesn't make speckles," she said slowly. "Speckles look like the rock froze while it was all mixed up. Like soup."

"Soup?" said Janelle, arriving with two granola bars and handing one to Maya, who had skipped lunch and was obviously hungry.

"Liquid soup. If soup cools, everything in it gets stuck where it is." Maya pointed at the speckles. "I think this was melted once. Molten rock. Then it cooled and hardened, and the speckles got trapped." She checked her field guide under "igneous," and there it was, a picture of speckled rock, the equivalent of the one in her hand.

"So it's igneous?" Scarlett asked.

"It's igneous," Maya said, placing it in the third pile with the dark rock she'd found near the old lava flow up the trail. Then she cleaned her hands on her jeans, stacked the three piles neatly on the flat stone, and looked up at the sun sinking toward the ridge. "Two minutes till four. Ready?"

Janelle raised her hand like she was answering a question in class. "Presenting our findings," she announced, and Maya laughed and waved Mr. Esposito over.

fact: Metals such as copper conduct electricity well, while plastic and rubber are insulators, which is why wires are copper covered in plastic.
story:
William pressed the battery into its clip, flipped the little switch, and stared at a bulb that refused to do anything except sit there. Around him the science museum's electronics room buzzed with other kids' successful circuits, which felt personal. He had enrolled in the Saturday workshop specifically to build this thing, and so far his foundation of confidence was cracking like an old sidewalk.

"Mine glows like a tiny sun," announced Abraham from the next stool, holding his board up. "Want me to get Ms. Weiss?"

"No. I can figure it out." William bent close to his circuit. The battery was fresh. The switch clicked properly. He traced the wire from one terminal to the bulb holder, then the second wire back to the switch. Everything looked connected. But looks, he was starting to suspect, were the whole problem. The thing that made a circuit work was invisible, the actual electricity, flowing somewhere he couldn't watch.

Brynley leaned over from across the table. "Your wires look different from mine. Fatter."

William picked one up. Where it bent, the red plastic coating had split, and inside was a strand of shiny copper. He turned it under the light. So the wire was really two things: a copper core and a plastic shell. He remembered his dad's kitchen tongs, plastic handles, and the plug at home that had shocked him once when the rubber cap was missing. A slow idea formed. Maybe electricity could travel through metal but not through plastic or rubber. That would be why wires were copper covered in plastic: the copper carried the current, and the covering kept it safe. So somewhere in his circuit, copper was not touching copper.

He examined every connection. At the switch, the wire's plastic end was clamped snugly under the screw instead of the metal inside. The plastic was blocking the flow, like a locked door in a hallway. He took the small clippers, stripped the end until bright copper showed, and screwed it down tight. He flipped the switch.

The bulb glowed. William whooped so loudly that Abraham dropped his own board, and the bulb survived, which was almost unanimous good luck.

"See?" Brynley said, grinning. "Invisible stuff, real proof."

William held his circuit up next to Abraham's tiny sun. "Mine's a tiny moon."
